_comment: Every deliberate difference between a binding's public names and docs/reference/bindings-v1.md, each with its written reason. Read by scripts/parity-surface.py (the parity gate, public issue #436); CONTRIBUTING.md's 'Changing a public name' says when an entry belongs here and when the doc or the bindings should change instead.

kind 'extra': public names the doc does not give (globs allowed, in the binding's own spelling: Owner.member, Owner.method(kw=) for a Python keyword-only parameter). kind 'missing': names the doc gives that the binding lacks (the doc's spelling). kind 'spelling': the doc's name `doc` that the binding spells `as`.
An entry, or a name in one, that matches nothing fails the gate as stale: remove it with the difference it explained.
An entry that hides a real gap, not a deliberate difference, carries `issue`: the public issue its fix waits on. `parity-surface.py --check-issues` fails once that issue is closed.

entries.reason: CHS_EXPORT_NONE (-1), the description's export-off constant, typed Format so that WithExport(ExportNone) type-checks. Python and TypeScript spell it EXPORT_NONE at module level (their own entries), and Rust's `export: Option<Format>` says it with None. Not a format: the vocabulary check counts Format's members without it.

§3 names the fact `ch_name`, which principle 2 spells ChName in Go (as §4 does for CallError.ChName), but the generated Go vocabulary (scripts/abi-v1/emit/go_vocab.py) treats CH as an initialism. Renaming a published method is a breaking change, so the difference is carried here rather than fixed in this gate's pull request.

The named types WithColumns and WithSettings return: one value implements several option interfaces (§2's call options: WithSettings implements CompileOption, RowOption, RowsOption, BlockOption, FilterOption and EvalOption), which Go's functional options can only express with a named type. The other three bindings carry the same options as fields, so they have nothing to name.

Go has one ArtifactError for the loader's refusals and the fetch layer's errors (§4: 'the fetch layer's and the loader's errors are one family'), so it also carries the fetch error's message, the platform, request and source it was answering, and the wrapped cause (Unwrap). §4 names only the refusal's fields.

The typed values of ArtifactError.Code, which §4's Go column names (`*ArtifactError` with `Code` CHTYPES_…): one constant per code in spec/fetch-v1/constants.json, re-exported from the fetch layer, with the code's CLI exit status and sentinel. Python keeps the same codes as CODE_* constants (its own entry); §4 gives no spelling for them.

§6: the fetch options carry everything fetch-v1.md configures (bases, cache directory, system directories, trusted keys, token, allow-unsigned, offline, frozen, the lock path) 'under the fetch module's own names', which the doc names in prose and does not spell per language. LockWrite and Update are the lock's write and update modes of fetch-v1.md §6.

Go-only: the fetch layer's connect and idle-read timeouts (spec/fetch-v1/constants.json `timeouts`), settable on Go's FetchOptions alone. Principle 2 says this convenience belongs in all four or in none; it is carried here as found, not changed, because removing a published field is a breaking change.

CHS_EXPORT_NONE (-1), the description's export-off constant, at module level; Go types it as Format (ExportNone, its own entry). `export=None` already means no export in Python's Schema.rows, so this is a spelling of the constant, not a second way to call.

Generated from the description by scripts/abi-v1/gen.py: each string vocabulary's decoder from a document's text, with the description's fallback. The decoders use it; §3 names the vocabularies and their facts, not their decoders.
The fetch codes of spec/fetch-v1/constants.json, and each artifact class's code: the attribute §4's Go column calls ArtifactError's `Code` (Go's own entry). §4's Python column names the classes only.

Keyword-only constructor parameters of error classes the binding raises: they set §4's refusal fields (reason, path, want, got) and the fetch layer's retry hints. A caller catches these classes and does not construct them.
The fetch layer's retry hints on an unreachable source (fetch-v1.md §7, the retry table): whether a retry may help, and the server's Retry-After. §4 names the class, not its fields.

§6: the fetch options carry everything fetch-v1.md configures (bases, cache directory, system directories, trusted keys, token, allow-unsigned, offline, frozen, the lock path) 'under the fetch module's own names', which the doc names in prose and does not spell per language. lock_write and update are the lock's write and update modes of fetch-v1.md §6.

Python's trusted keys are TrustedKey records (key id and raw public key) where Go's FetchOptions.TrustedKeys takes hex strings: a shape difference inside §6's 'trusted keys', carried as found. Changing either is a breaking change.

The package's implementation modules, public by name. Every public name they hold is re-exported at the top level (measured by this gate: it lists any that is not), and the top level is what the doc describes and the gate compares.

Found by this gate: the binding's own constructors for InternalError and UsageError, listed in chtypes.errors.__all__ and so public through the submodule, though the package does not re-export them and the doc gives neither. Dropping them from __all__ is a public-API change for its own pull request; carried here until then.

Found by this gate: rust/src/result.rs declares `pub struct EngineCell`, and BatchResult.engine_rows holds it, but lib.rs does not re-export it, so a caller cannot name chtypes::EngineCell (cargo-public-api lists no path to it). Re-exporting it is a public-API addition for its own pull request; carried here until then.

§3's `lossy` fact is a free function in Rust's `reason` module, spelled with Rust's is_ prefix for a predicate, as `source::is_stored` is (that fact's own name already starts with is_). The generated module (scripts/abi-v1/emit/rust.py) is published at 1.0, so renaming it is a breaking change.

Every format as an array, for iteration: Rust enums cannot be iterated, where Python iterates the IntEnum and TypeScript the const object's values. Not a format: the vocabulary check counts Format's members without it.

A string vocabulary's document spelling. Rust's vocabularies are enums, so the text is a method, where Python's StrEnum member and TypeScript's const-object value are the string itself and Go's type is a string. Generated from the description by scripts/abi-v1/gen.py.
The flag set's raw bits, in and out: Rust's DocFlags is a newtype, where Go's, Python's (IntFlag) and TypeScript's flags are numbers already. Generated from the description by scripts/abi-v1/gen.py.

The five call-error fields from whichever of the four call variants an Error is: Rust's spelling of Go's AsCallError and of catching Python's and TypeScript's CallError base, which §4 names for those languages (for Rust it says 'Rust's match').
The fetch code of an artifact variant (spec/fetch-v1/constants.json): the Rust spelling of Go's ArtifactError.Code and Python's `.code` (their own entries). §4 gives no Rust spelling.
Rust's collection idiom (clippy's len_without_is_empty) beside iter() and IntoIterator, which §5 names; Python's ErrorCodeTable has __len__ for the same fact, which the gate treats as protocol.

§3: Rust keeps v0's RawText for every byte output, with the bytes, as_bytes(), as_str() -> Option<&str> and a lossy Display (named in §3's prose, not a table). The rest are its byte-string helpers. The other bindings' byte type is the language's own (string, bytes, Buffer), so they have nothing to name.

Rust's loader refusal carries a free-text detail beside §4's reason, path, want and got (noted in the 1.0 comparison, #435). It is Rust-only, carried as found: removing a published field is a breaking change.

§6: the fetch options carry everything fetch-v1.md configures (bases, cache directory, system directories, trusted keys, token, allow-unsigned, offline, frozen, the lock path) 'under the fetch module's own names', which the doc names in prose and does not spell per language. lock_write and update are the lock's write and update modes of fetch-v1.md §6.

Rust-only: the platform to fetch for, where the other bindings fetch for the host. Principle 2 says this belongs in all four or in none; it is carried here as found, not changed, because removing a published field is a breaking change.

§3's vocabularies are const objects in TypeScript (`Format.JSONEachRow` is a number, not an object), which cannot carry a member, so each fact is a free function named for its vocabulary (the 1.0 comparison, #435). Generated from the description by scripts/abi-v1/gen.py; a rename is a breaking change.

Generated from the description by scripts/abi-v1/gen.py; a rename is a breaking change.

TypeScript keeps a loader refusal's fields (§4: reason, path, want, got) on the classes a refusal raises, ArtifactIncompatibleError and LoaderCorruptError (both implement LoaderErrorFields; their own entry), not on the ArtifactError base the fetch layer's errors share, which carries the code. §4 names the carrier for Go (*ArtifactError) and Rust (Refusal) only; the gate reads Go's for TypeScript and Python, and Python's base does carry them.

Where TypeScript keeps §4's refusal fields (see its `missing` entry for ArtifactError): LoaderCorruptError is the loader's corrupt refusal, a subclass of ArtifactCorruptError so that catching ArtifactCorruptError still catches both (§4's one family); TypeScript-only, noted in the 1.0 comparison (#435). LoaderErrorFields is the interface both refusal classes implement.

The fetch code (spec/fetch-v1/constants.json) and its CLI exit status: TypeScript's spelling of Go's ArtifactError.Code and ErrorCode.ExitCode, Python's `.code` and Rust's Error.code (their own entries). §4 gives no TypeScript spelling.

The interface of §4's five call-error fields, which CallError implements and its constructors take: a type-level name for the same fields, so it adds no field. The other bindings spell the fields once, on CallError (Go's struct, Python's class, Rust's struct).

The description's batch_outcome vocabulary on its own, generated by scripts/abi-v1/gen.py and exported by TypeScript alone; §3 folds row_outcome and batch_outcome into one Outcome, which TypeScript also exports. TypeScript-only, carried as found: removing an export is a breaking change.

The description's discover_query_param vocabulary (the discovery query's two parameters, which §5 names in prose), generated by scripts/abi-v1/gen.py and exported by TypeScript alone. TypeScript-only, carried as found: removing an export is a breaking change.

CHS_EXPORT_NONE (-1), the description's export-off constant, as Python spells it (its own entry); Go types it as Format (ExportNone). An absent exportFormat already means no export in TypeScript's RowsOptions.

TypeScript's iteration protocol over the table, beside all(): the counterpart of Rust's IntoIterator, which §5 names. The gate counts TypeScript's [Symbol.dispose] as a name because §2 and §3 name it, so this one is listed rather than treated as protocol.

The fetch layer's retry hint on an unreachable source (fetch-v1.md §7, the retry table): the Retry-After the client refused to wait for. Python carries retryable and retry_after instead (its own entry): the two bindings differ here, carried as found.

True for any error the package throws on purpose. TypeScript's ArtifactError (the fetch layer's error class, re-exported) does not extend ChtypesError, so one guard covers the call errors and the artifact errors together; Python's ArtifactError is a ChtypesError, Go has no base and Rust has one Error enum, so none of them needs it. TypeScript-only, carried as found.
